source: Wikipedia (2026) Psychology of programming
finding: Field also called empirical studies of programmers (ESP). Grew from late 1970s and early 1980s when tool usability, not just compute power, became the thing to evaluate. Two workshop series: ESP (US) and PPIG (Europe).
numbers: Research methods section is one line: introspection, observation, experiment, qualitative research.
quote: Some methods ... include introspection, observation, experiment, and qualitative research.
limits: Encyclopedia page. The methods section is a list with no evidence behind it.
agent_relevance: Background only. The four-method list is a useful taxonomy for labelling what kind of evidence a claim about programmers rests on.

source: Wikipedia (2026) Protocol analysis
finding: Protocol analysis elicits verbal reports from participants to study thinking. Used in cognitive psychology, cognitive science, behaviour analysis, usability and design research. Foundational text: Ericsson and Simon (1993) Protocol analysis: Verbal reports as data.
numbers: No numbers. Names Crutcher 1994, Simon and Kaplan 1989, Gero and McNeill 1998 (design protocols).
limits: Short page. Does not give the validity evidence.
agent_relevance: Our agent's own reasoning trace is a verbal protocol. Same rules apply: what is verbalised from working memory is data; invented explanations are not.

source: Wikipedia (2026) Think-aloud protocol
finding: Think-aloud was brought into usability testing by Clayton Lewis at IBM, derived from Ericsson and Simon protocol analysis. Practitioners depart from Ericsson and Simon: they prompt more often, which risks changing what participants say.
numbers: Page suggests about 5 participants are usually enough for usability work.
limits: The 5-participant rule is a usability heuristic, not a statistical power claim.
agent_relevance: Prompting a model mid-reasoning is the same departure: extra probes change the trace.

source: Wikipedia (2026) Introspection illusion
finding: People think they have direct insight into the causes of their mental states but treat others' introspection as unreliable. Evidence suggests introspection is construction and inference. Coined by Emily Pronin; four components.
numbers: No effect sizes on the page. Says evidence is arguably inadequate to decide how reliable introspection is in normal conditions.
limits: Summary page only. Debated.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule for the agent: self-explanations are not proof of the real cause. Check them against behaviour.

source: Nisbett and Wilson (1977) Telling more than we can know: verbal reports on mental processes
finding: People often cannot report the real causes of their choices and instead give plausible theories. In the stocking study, shoppers chose the right-most of four identical items far more often, and none cited position.
numbers: Recalled, not read this session: about 52 shoppers; choice rose from about 12% (left) to about 40% (right). Treat figures as approximate.
limits: Not opened. Later work (Ericsson and Simon) argues that concurrent reports of what is in attention differ from retrospective reasons.
agent_relevance: Do not trust the agent's stated reason for an answer as the cause. Test it by changing the input and seeing if the answer changes.

source: Ericsson and Simon (1980) Verbal reports as data
finding: Model: verbal reports are valid data when they report the contents of short-term memory in the order they are used. Plain think-aloud (direct verbalisation) should not change the process. Asking for explanations or reasons does change it.
numbers: No numbers recalled with confidence.
limits: Not opened. Retrospective reports are most at risk. Only covers tasks with verbalisable content.
agent_relevance: Maps onto LLM traces: a reasoning trace emitted during the work is closer to a valid protocol than a post-hoc justification.

source: Ericsson and Simon (1993) Protocol analysis: verbal reports as data (revised)
finding: Book-length treatment of coding verbal protocols: record, transcribe, segment, code with a scheme, then check reliability. Three levels of verbalisation: direct, encoding, explanation.
numbers: None opened.
limits: Not opened. Cited via Wikipedia and via Enoiu et al. (2020), which uses its procedure.
agent_relevance: The segment-code-agree pipeline is what an LLM annotator must replace or support (see a11).

source: Fox, Ericsson and Best (2011) Do procedures for verbal reporting of thinking have to be reactive? Psychological Bulletin
finding: Meta-analysis of studies comparing think-aloud with silent work. Reported that ordinary think-aloud does not change accuracy of performance; explanation-type reporting can.
numbers: Recalled: about 94 studies. Treat count as approximate.
limits: Not opened. Real result may include a small time cost.
agent_relevance: Backs using visible reasoning traces as data without assuming they distort the answer, while still avoiding forced rationales.

source: Enoiu, Tukseferi and Feldt (2020) Towards a model of testers' cognitive processes
finding: Builds a problem-solving model of test design and tests it with think-aloud verbal protocols. Segments are coded against hypothesised steps (test goal, analyse knowledge, form strategy, organise information, allocate resources, monitor, evaluate). Every step appeared in all subjects except feelings (4 of 5).
numbers: 5 master students. Mean share of coded activity (%): test goal 7.1, analyse knowledge 5.4, form strategy 13.1, organise information 16.1 (order as in the table I read; row labels may be shifted), allocate resources 10.3 or 5.1, monitor 2.6, evaluate 6.3, silence 27.6, feelings 1.0, N/A 5.3. Text says test goal about 12% of time, analyse knowledge 39%, allocate resources 5.1%, monitor and evaluate 9%.
limits: Pilot with N=5 students on one program (bowling game). Table text came out garbled; the in-text percentages and the table do not match cleanly, so use only the pattern. No inter-coder statistics seen. Confirmatory only; no competing model.
agent_relevance: A worked example of protocol analysis in programming. The step list is a candidate checklist for the agent's test-design phase.

source: Sjoberg and Bergersen (2018) The price of using students (comment on Falessi et al.)
finding: Argues students are fine subjects but skill differs from professionals, and skill moderates treatment effects, so conclusions can flip (the reversal effect). Pair programming helped juniors but hurt seniors; design patterns hurt students but helped experienced professionals.
numbers: Skill curves from three experiments, n=262 professionals (Arisholm and Sjoberg 2004; Arisholm et al. 2007; Bergersen et al. 2014). Student curves are hypothesised, not measured.
limits: Position paper. Student skill distribution is assumed from the law of practice, not data.
agent_relevance: A method that helps novices may hurt experts. Scaffolds for the agent should be tested across difficulty, not only on average.

source: Falessi et al. (2018) Empirical software engineering experts on the use of students and professionals in experiments
finding: Experts say papers get rejected for using students. Authors argue that students are acceptable when the research question and the target population match.
numbers: Quote reported in Sjoberg and Bergersen: 'too many times that our papers were rejected because we used students'.
limits: Not opened; known only through the comment paper.
agent_relevance: Same logic for LLM stand-ins for participants: ask whether the stand-in matches the target population.

source: Ahmed, Devanbu, Treude and Pradel (2025) Can LLMs replace manual annotation of software engineering artifacts?
finding: Six LLMs rated ten annotation tasks from five prior human-subject datasets. LLM-human agreement was often close to human-human agreement. Model-model agreement predicted whether LLMs suit a task.
numbers: Krippendorff alpha. Code summaries: model-model 0.68-0.76; human-model 0.24-0.40 vs human-human 0.21-0.48. Semantic similarity: human-human 0.71-0.83, human-model 0.64-0.77, model-model 0.69-0.83. Causality: human-human 0.44, human-model 0.22, model-model 0.39. Static analysis warning model-model 0.12. Spearman of model-model vs human-model 0.65 (p<0.05).
limits: Ten tasks only. Fails on causality and static-analysis judgments. Low agreement among models warns not to substitute.
agent_relevance: Use agreement between several model runs as a cheap check of whether a judgment is reliable. Where models disagree, escalate.

source: Ahmed et al. (2025) confidence-based partial replacement (same paper, RQ3 and RQ4)
finding: Replacing one human rating with an LLM rating, on samples chosen by model confidence, keeps inter-rater agreement better than random selection. Up to about 50% to 60% of ratings could be replaced on some datasets without a significant change.
numbers: Replaceable fraction: up to 60% on causality, 50% on static analysis warning; confidence selection beat random except at 100%. Model-model agreement was 0.66-0.82 on tasks where humans and models agreed.
limits: Cutoff for confidence must be chosen per task; confidence helps even when model-model agreement is low, for about half the data, but the cutoff stays open.
agent_relevance: Route only low-confidence items to a human or a stronger check. Matches our confidence-gated design.

source: Leca, Valenca, Santos and de Souza Santos (2024) LLMs in qualitative analysis: a mapping study for empirical SE
finding: Systematic mapping of 20 studies of LLMs in qualitative analysis. Main uses: coding, thematic analysis, categorisation. Benefits: speed and help for new researchers. Limits: output variability, weak on nuance, privacy and transparency worries.
numbers: 20 studies. Tool lists in Table III: ChatGPT (version unspecified) in 11 studies, GPT-3.5 in 5, GPT-4 in 5, Claude 1, LLaMA-13B 1, Mixtral 1 (some studies use more than one).
limits: Mapping study, not a pooled effect. Only 20 papers, mostly outside software engineering.
agent_relevance: Outputs vary run to run, so use repeated runs and compare, not a single pass.

source: Khojah, Mohamad, Leitner and Gomes de Oliveira Neto (2024) Beyond code generation: observational study of ChatGPT in SE practice
finding: Qualitative observation of 24 engineers using ChatGPT for a week. People used it more for guidance and learning than for ready code. Proposes a framework: purpose, internal factors (personality, expectations), external factors (policy).
numbers: 24 engineers at 10 companies; chats split into 208 dialogues, 180 relevant to software engineering. Expert consultation is 62% of dialogues; used at least once by all but two participants.
limits: GPT-3.5 only, one week, self-selected participants, qualitative coding by authors.
agent_relevance: Real use leans on advice and explanation, not generation. Supports building the agent as a thinking partner.

source: Becker et al. / METR (2025) Measuring the impact of early-2025 AI on experienced open-source developer productivity
finding: Randomised controlled trial in the field. Developers forecast AI would cut time by 24%, estimated afterward 20%, but AI-allowed tasks took 19% longer. Experts predicted 39% (economics) and 38% (ML) shorter.
numbers: 16 developers, 246 tasks averaging 2.0 hours, repos with about 23,000 stars. Developers averaged 5 years and 1,500 commits in their repo; paid $150/hour. 93% had used LLMs; 44% had used Cursor before.
limits: Small number of developers, one tool set (Cursor Pro, Claude 3.5/3.7), early 2025, experienced users on familiar large repos. Authors checked 21 factors; 5 have evidence of contributing to slowdown.
agent_relevance: Self-report and expert forecast were wrong in sign. Do not trust the agent's or a user's felt benefit; measure.

source: Becker et al. (2025) screen-recording check on compliance and mechanisms
finding: Screen recordings let the authors check cheating and use. AI was unused in only 16.4% of labeled AI-allowed videos; AI use in AI-disallowed tasks was about 6%. With AI, less time coding and searching, more prompting, waiting, reviewing; about 9% of time cleaning AI output.
numbers: 44 valid AI-allowed and 54 AI-disallowed labeled recordings for compliance; 128 recordings (143 hours) labeled for activity; 3 cheating cases of 54. No meaningful difference by prior AI experience.
limits: Subset of tasks only. Screen video is observation of behaviour, not of thought.
agent_relevance: Observation of behaviour (what was done) beats self-report; log the agent's actions, not only its story.

source: Borg et al. (2024) Does co-development with AI assistants lead to more maintainable code? Registered report
finding: Registered report for a two-phase study: Phase 1 adds a feature with or without an AI assistant; Phase 2 is an RCT where new developers evolve the Phase 1 code without AI. Uses the GQM model and Bayesian analysis.
numbers: Outcomes: completion time, perceived productivity, code quality, test coverage.
limits: Plan only; results are in a20 (Borg et al. 2026).
agent_relevance: Pre-register what counts as success before running an agent benchmark.

source: Borg et al. (2026) Echoes of AI: downstream effects of AI assistants on maintainability
finding: Preregistered two-phase experiment. No significant differences in later evolution time or code quality when other developers worked on AI co-developed code. Phase 1 observational: AI users were faster.
numbers: 151 participants, 95% professional developers. Phase 1: 30.7% median reduction in completion time; habitual AI users estimated 55.9% speedup. Phase 2 frequentist tests underpowered for small effects (power about 0.17 for d=0.2), so Bayesian analysis added: any gain was at most small and uncertain.
limits: Short Java task, no AI in Phase 2. Observational Phase 1 is open to confounding.
agent_relevance: Speed gains do not show harm to maintainability here. But check downstream effects, not just first-pass speed.

source: Kaufman, Brun, Murali and Endres (2026) Programmers are poor and overconfident judges of LLM-generated assertions
finding: Controlled experiment with a think-aloud follow-up. Programmers judged correct assertions at 74% accuracy but incorrect ones at 49%, with similar confidence. Natural-language explanations gave no overall benefit, and weak ones raised confidence.
numbers: 86 Python programmers; 260 stimuli; OR=2.94 (p<0.001); confidence 3.99 vs 4.25 of 5 (p=0.005) for low-quality explanations; 10 think-aloud participants.
limits: Single task type (assertions on HumanEval functions), recruited from universities and snowball sampling.
agent_relevance: Explanations from a model can increase trust without increasing correctness. The agent should not use its own explanation as evidence of being right.

source: Hak, Johnson, Amoozadeh, Alipour and Chattopadhyay (2025) Observing without doing: pseudo-apprenticeship in student LLM use
finding: Think-aloud plus survey and interview with CS1 students. Students read expert LLM solutions but skip the steps that build independent skill. Gaps appeared between what students said they did and what recordings showed.
numbers: 14 undergraduates, 3 tasks. LLM use 64% (9/14) on the familiar task and 86% (12/14) on each of the other two. Debugger use: 43% self-reported, 0 observed; LLMs used for debugging by 57%, print statements by 36%.
limits: 14 students, mixed methods, qualitative coding; not randomised.
agent_relevance: Self-report versus observed behaviour diverged. Same gap matters for an agent describing its own method.

source: Enoiu et al. (2020) proposed experiment design (protocol steps)
finding: Pipeline: record, transcribe, divide into segments (phrases, sentences, clauses), encode against predicates, then content and pattern analysis. Participants think aloud while testing a program from a specification.
numbers: Encoding scheme of 11 categories incl. silence and N/A (behaviour that could not be coded).
limits: Pilot only.
agent_relevance: The same pipeline can be run on an LLM trace with an LLM or rule coder, using the Ahmed et al. agreement checks (a12).

source: Khojah et al. (2024) analytic method note
finding: Method used: manual split of chat logs into dialogues, then qualitative coding of purpose, plus an exit survey, then a theory-building step. A mixed design of log observation plus survey.
numbers: 208 dialogues to 180; outliers checked by prompts per dialogue over time.
limits: Author-team coding; no agreement figure seen in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Log-based observation can be done on agent runs at scale without human subjects.

source: Leca et al. (2024) implications note
finding: Authors conclude human expertise is still needed to interpret data and call for structured guidelines for LLM use in qualitative research in software engineering.
numbers: Qualitative methods named: grounded theory, ethnography, action research.
limits: Recommendation, not tested.
agent_relevance: Use the LLM for first-pass coding; keep a human or second method for interpretation.

source: Hak et al. (2025) method note: tasks varied by familiarity
finding: Task familiarity changed LLM use: no one used an LLM for code writing in the familiar task, but code-writing prompts came early and often in the unfamiliar one. Open-ended task showed the widest variation (4 brainstorm, 5 short syntax questions, 2 heavy code writing).
numbers: As counted in the paper: 4 + 5 + 2 participants in the open-ended activity.
limits: Small N; counts are descriptive.
agent_relevance: Reliance on help rises with task novelty. The agent may over-lean on tools on unfamiliar problems.
